comments.text: Budget billing sounds like billing averaging. They take the total you pay for a year, divide by 12 and that's how much you pay monthly instead of paying extremely high bills in winter and low in summer, it's to help people by making the monthly bill the same every month. As such, a person will get "behind" depending on when they started it, but they get caught up once the entire year has gone by. This is why he is griping about having to pay $700 to end the billing, he used a lot of power he didn't pay for over winter because the billing was averaged over a year, come summer the usage will be lower but he'll still pay the average amount and get caught up (in essence paying the $700 over the lower cost summer months) Bottom line, he underpays his bills in the winter and overpays in the summer in order to have the same bill every month.

comments.author: @solomongrundysfoot
comments.text:
Budget billing means you are carrying a debt from the expensive months spread out through the cheap months, you carry the average throughout the year (plus an extra month, I think). Gotta time your cancel after the cheap months when you true-up (before summer high usage or before winter high usage). If you have to call to ask how much power you're using like this without trying to understand, then you pretty much don't care and just want to complain when you might have developed a bad usage habit, or have lack of insulation in your home, or bad a/c motor, or (like my parents discovered) a disconnected air duct in the attic causing $500+ summer bills.

Get a copy of your bills and study them to see what your cost per kWh is. Then look over a year's worth to see what the trends are. Take a look at your meter to make sure it matches your bill. Then, if necessary, take an ammeter to your panel and see if there are any suspicious high current appliances. 

My point is while you are absolutely justified being worried about high cost, you sound dumb like you have no time to invest why your house is using that much. Treat this like any other home repair, like a water/roof leak, etc. when something isn't working right, investigate and replace/repair. Talking to someone on the phone is not going to find the problem.

comments.author: @RMartin631
comments.text: I have budget billing and I love it. Once a year (in my case it's December) they take my previous 12 months of electric usage, and divide it by 12. You should still look at your bill every month so you can identify a problem that you may have. In January and February of '24, my actual usage spiked way up. My heat pump stopped working properly, and the backup heat strips were heating my house. In March I replaced the heat pump, and my actual usage dropped considerably. The next year's budget billing went up as I expected it to. This year's budget billing dropped way back down, since I now have a high-efficiency Carrier heat pump. You have to be real about why your electric bill is so high. The real energy suckers are heating and AC, stoves, clothes dryers, water heaters, and any high wattage lights that you may have. I have a 2,500 sq foot house. We have an apartment included in our sq footage and on our electric bill. We have 2 full kitchens, 2 water heaters, and 2 heat pumps. We have 8 LED lights outside of the house that stay on from dusk to dawn. Our budget billing is $194 per month.
